items.followUp: Use the kinetic molecular model to explain why a gas can be compressed more easily than a liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the basic kinetic molecular model used to explain the states of matter.
rubric.description: States that matter consists of particles in continuous motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that matter is made of moving particles.

rubric.why: Checks the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid.
rubric.description: Describes solid particles as closely packed and vibrating about fixed positions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate description of solid particles.

rubric.why: Checks how particle motion and forces distinguish a liquid from a solid.
rubric.description: Describes liquid particles as able to move past one another because the forces are weaker.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate description of liquid particles.

rubric.why: Checks the particle arrangement, motion and forces in a gas.
rubric.description: Describes gas particles as far apart and moving freely or randomly, with very weak forces between them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate description of gas particles.

modelAnswer: Matter consists of tiny particles that are in continuous motion and exert forces on one another.
In a solid, particles are closely packed; strong forces hold them in fixed positions, where they vibrate.
In a liquid, particles are less closely packed and can slide past one another because the forces are weaker.
In a gas, particles are far apart, move freely and randomly, and have very weak forces between them.
Differences in particle arrangement, motion and forces explain the different properties of the states of matter.

items.followUp: Why is it important to use the same standard unit when comparing measurements made by different people?

rubric.why: Checks that standard units provide a shared basis for comparing measurements.
rubric.description: Explains that a standard unit allows measurements to be compared on a common basis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the common comparison purpose of standard units.

rubric.why: Checks that standard units make measurements understandable and reliable.
rubric.description: Explains that standard units are universally accepted, avoid confusion, or give consistent results.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid benefit of using standard units.

modelAnswer: A standard unit provides a common basis for comparing measurements.
Standard units are universally accepted and give consistent results, avoiding confusion when measurements are recorded or communicated.

items.followUp: State two effects a force can have on the motion of an object.

rubric.why: Checks that a force can change an object's speed or state of motion.
rubric.description: States that a force can start or stop an object, or change its speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct change in speed or state of motion.

rubric.why: Checks that a force can change the direction in which an object moves.
rubric.description: States that a force can change an object's direction of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a change in direction.

modelAnswer: A force may start or stop an object, or change its speed.
A force may also change the direction of an object's motion.

items.followUp: Explain what happens to a boat when a person jumps from it onto the river bank, using Newton's third law.

rubric.why: Checks the force exerted by the jumper on the boat as they jump.
rubric.description: States that the jumper pushes the boat backward, producing an action-reaction pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the backward push or action-reaction interaction.

rubric.why: Checks the boat's backward motion and how it can prevent the jumper from reaching the bank.
rubric.description: Explains that the boat moves away from the bank, increasing the separation so the jumper may miss the bank and fall into the water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the boat's recoil and its consequence for the jumper.

modelAnswer: As the person jumps, they push the boat backward with their feet.
The boat recoils away from the river bank, increasing the separation; the jumper may then miss the bank and fall into the water.
